topic: Solving Simultaneous Linear Equations by Substitution

lessonData.topic: Solving Simultaneous Linear Equations by Substitution
lessonData.subject: Mathematics / Geometry
lessonData.tagline: Unlock two unknowns by turning a two-variable puzzle into a single solvable equation!
lessonData.overview: The substitution method solves simultaneous equations by isolating one variable in terms of the other and swapping it into the second equation. This strategic move eliminates one unknown, reducing a two-variable system into a straightforward single-variable linear equation.

chalkNotes.title: Mastering the Substitution Method
chalkNotes.subtitle: Two Equations, Two Unknowns -> One Equation, One Unknown
chalkNotes.coreRuleOrFormula: If y = expression(x), replace every 'y' in the OTHER equation with (expression(x)).
bulletPoints: Select smart: Always isolate a variable with a coefficient of 1 or -1 (e.g., y in 4x + y = 57) to keep steps clean.
Bracket rule: Never write -2 * 57 - 4x; write -2(57 - 4x) so the -2 distributes to both terms (+8x).
Avoid the echo loop: Never plug your expression back into the exact same equation it came from—you will just get 0 = 0 or 57 = 57.
Dual verification: A true solution (x, y) must satisfy BOTH original equations when checked.
keyTakeaways: Substitution works by combining two distinct lines of information into a single one-variable equation.
Parentheses are non-negotiable when substituting expressions with two or more terms.

quiz.question: Given the simultaneous equations: (1) 7x - 2y = 21 and (2) 4x + y = 57. A student isolates y from equation (2) as y = 57 - 4x. Which of the following shows the correct next step?
quiz.explanation: To combine the two equations, substitute (57 - 4x) for y into equation (1), not equation (2). Parentheses are essential around (57 - 4x) so the factor -2 correctly multiplies both 57 and -4x. Option B misses the brackets (failing to distribute -2 across both terms). Option C substitutes back into equation (2), which simplifies trivially to 57 = 57 without revealing the values. Option D mistakenly substitutes the expression for x instead of y.

suggestedQuestions: Prerequisite Diagnostic: How do you make y the subject of the equation 4x + y = 57?
Misconception Probe: What happens algebraically if you substitute y = 57 - 4x back into 4x + y = 57 instead of equation (1)?
Deeper Application: What strategy should we use if every variable has a coefficient other than 1 or -1 (e.g., 3x + 5y = 11 and 2x - 7y = 9)?

solving-simultaneous-linear-equations-by.title: Solving Systems by Substitution
solving-simultaneous-linear-equations-by.description: A step-by-step procedure to solve two linear equations by isolating one variable and substituting it into the other.

nodes.label: Isolate One Variable
nodes.details: Select the equation with the simplest variable (coefficient of 1 or -1) and rearrange it to get that variable by itself.

nodes.label: Substitute into Other Equation
nodes.details: Insert the isolated expression into the untouched equation using parentheses to create an equation with only one variable.

nodes.label: Solve Single-Variable Equation
nodes.details: Simplify and use inverse operations to determine the exact numerical value of the remaining variable.

nodes.label: Back-Substitute to Find Pair
nodes.details: Plug the solved numerical value back into the isolated formula to calculate the second variable and state the solution pair.

key-properties-of-solving-simultaneous-l.title: Solving Systems by Substitution: Core Mechanics
key-properties-of-solving-simultaneous-l.description: A step-by-step pathway illustrating how the substitution method reduces a two-variable system into a solvable single-variable equation.

nodes.label: Isolate a Variable
nodes.details: Rearrange one equation so a single variable is expressed in terms of the other, ideally choosing a variable with a coefficient of 1 or -1.

nodes.label: Substitute into Other Equation
nodes.details: Plug the isolated expression into the remaining equation, eliminating one unknown and leaving a single-variable linear equation.

nodes.label: Solve Single Variable
nodes.details: Solve the standard 1-variable linear equation using inverse operations to find the precise numerical value of that variable.

nodes.label: Back-Substitute for Ordered Pair
nodes.details: Substitute the found value back into the isolated equation to calculate the second variable and write the intersection point (x, y).

nodes.label: Direct Variable Substitution

nodes.details: Plugs the isolated real-world variable into the second equation, reducing two unknowns to one easily solvable equation.

main.title: Substitution: The Player Swap
main.why: It shows that substitution is a physical replacement of a variable with an equivalent algebraic expression, maintaining the balance of the equation.
main.checkQuestion: Why must we put the (57 - 4x) inside brackets when substituting it into the first equation?

steps.name: Identify the swap
steps.caption: We isolate 'y' in the second equation to see its 'teammate' expression.

steps.name: Perform substitution
steps.caption: We remove 'y' from the first equation and replace it with its teammate inside brackets.

steps.name: Highlight safety rule
steps.caption: Using brackets ensures we multiply everything correctly, avoiding common sign errors.

contrast:substituting-into-same-equation.title: Testing the Substitution Rule
contrast:substituting-into-same-equation.why: This shows that substituting into the same equation creates a logical loop that leads nowhere, whereas switching to the other equation uses the full system of information.
contrast:substituting-into-same-equation.checkQuestion: When we substitute into the SAME equation, we get 0=0; what does this tell us about using information from both equations?

steps.name: Anchor the system
steps.caption: We have two equations for two unknowns.

steps.name: Test the same equation
steps.caption: What happens if we rearrange Eq 1 and put it back into itself?

steps.name: Test the other equation
steps.caption: Now let's bridge Eq 1 into Eq 2 to combine the information.

steps.name: Check for understanding
steps.caption: Compare the two results; why does one lead to an answer and the other to 0 = 0?

contrast:substituting-into-same-equation.focus: Substituting an expression back into the exact same equation it was derived from will find the value of the variable.

contrast:forgetting-brackets-in-substitu.title: Substitution: Why Brackets Matter
contrast:forgetting-brackets-in-substitu.why: This visual comparison makes it clear that without brackets, the multiplier only hits the first term, ignoring the full value of the substituted expression.
contrast:forgetting-brackets-in-substitu.checkQuestion: In the bracketed version, why does the second part become +8x instead of -4x?

steps.name: Establish the goal
steps.caption: Let's explore what happens when we substitute the entire expression for y.

steps.name: Show the common mix-up
steps.caption: If we don't use brackets, does the -2 multiply every part of the expression?

steps.name: Show the working rule
steps.caption: When we add brackets, watch how the negative sign distributes to both terms.

steps.name: Ask to compare
steps.caption: Look at the -114 - 4x versus -114 + 8x; what changed in the second term?

contrast:forgetting-brackets-in-substitu.focus: When substituting an expression with multiple terms, brackets are unnecessary.

apply.title: Applying Substitution
apply.why: Visualizing two distinct linear equations as lines helps the learner see that solving by substitution is finding the single shared point where both rules are satisfied.
apply.checkQuestion: Looking at the lines, does it look like there is only one specific point that works for both equations?
